nv_kraft_mountain_area.blurb: Kraft Mountain rises above Calico Basin in the Red Rocks canyon country of southern Nevada, and its sandstone walls and boulders hold a wide mix of styles. Trad is the most common, with sport not far behind and a modest set of boulder problems at the easier V grades. Roped climbs run from about 5.6 to the low 5.13s, piled up between 5.10 and 5.12 with a thinner group of moderates. The lower band of Kraft Crags faces south and takes the sun all day, which keeps it pleasant when the weather is cool, while Sunny and Steep offers steep, powerful bolted climbing in sun from mid-morning to dusk. The sandstone is fragile when damp.

nh_wm_kancamagus_central.blurb: Kancamagus (Central) gathers the granite crags along the middle of the Kancamagus Highway in New Hampshire's White Mountains, led by Greens Cliff, Owl's Cliff and Table Mountain. Trad dominates, with a fair amount of sport and a handful of winter ice routes. Rock climbs run from about 5.5 to the low 5.13s, mostly between 5.8 and 5.12. Owl's Cliff is mostly solid granite walls reaching about 250 feet, with slabs, cracks, corners and arêtes, and it is quiet and remote. Table Mountain is a south-facing slab with both trad and bolted lines. Approaches vary widely, from under an hour at some crags to a long hike at others, so the region feels spread out and uncrowded.

tn_sunset_park.blurb: Sunset Park runs along the western face of Lookout Mountain in Chattanooga, Tennessee, a cliff of hard sandstone best known for single-pitch trad. Nearly everything is gear-protected, with a few aid lines and a pair of boulder problems. Grades stretch from about 5.4 to the low 5.13s, but most routes fall between 5.7 and 5.11, so intermediate leaders find plenty to climb, and many lines can also be top-roped. A few routes go to two pitches. The cliff stays shaded for much of the day, which makes it a favorite in summer, while winter days can be cold. The climbing divides into two sections of similar size, Sunset North and Sunset South.

ca_east_side.blurb: East Side is the part of Pinnacles National Park in California's central coast ranges that is entered from the park's east gate, with the main crags close to the Bear Gulch area. The rock is volcanic breccia, noticeably weaker than granite or basalt, so holds can snap off and natural protection is often scarce. Steep, bolted faces make up most of the climbing: sport is the largest share, with a solid portion of trad and a few top-ropes. Grades run from easy to about 5.14, with the most routes between 5.8 and 5.11. Discovery Wall is the largest and busiest crag, followed by the Monolith, Tourist Trap and the Sisters. Climbing is possible year-round, though temperatures swing sharply during a day.

ca_seki_bouldering.blurb: SEKI Bouldering scatters granite boulders through the forests of Sequoia and Kings Canyon national parks in the central Sierra Nevada, many sitting beside giant sequoias. Almost everything is bouldering, mostly slabs and vertical faces with a little overhanging terrain. Problems run from very easy to V8, but the bulk are V0 to V3, which suits relaxed circuits more than hard projecting. Cedar Grove, along the South Fork of the Kings River in the bottom of Kings Canyon, is by far the biggest cluster; Slickrock, Lodgepole and Wuksachi are smaller groups. The season depends on elevation: around 7,000 feet it runs roughly May through November, while foothill boulders at about 1,000 to 4,500 feet give winter and spring options.

co_10_mile_canyon.blurb: Ten Mile Canyon is a roadside collection of crags beside I-70 between Frisco and Copper Mountain, at about 9,200 feet. The rock is gneiss and granite of varying quality. Sport climbing is the main draw, backed by a good amount of trad, a bouldering zone, a few top-ropes, and a winter season of ice with some mixed lines. Rock climbs run from about 5.5 to the low 5.13s, mostly between 5.7 and 5.11, with plenty of moderates; boulder problems range from V0 to V7. White Cliff, Officer's Gulch West, Smile Wall and The Dome are among the larger crags. The ice at Officer's Gulch is mostly easy to moderate and best early in the season, since many lines sit at the bottom of avalanche chutes.
